documentation.range:
This species is restricted to the sagebrush shrublands of the interior northwest of North America, now almost confined to the USA with few remaining in Alberta and Saskatchewan in Canada. In the US the largest populations remain in Wyoming, Idaho, Montana and Nevada, with fewer in Oregon, Utah, North and South Dakota and Colorado. Isolated populations are found in Washington, Jackson’s Hole in central Wyoming and along the border of California and Nevada. The species has become extirpated from British Columbia. 
Based on the modelling of long-term lek-count data the population has been declining at a rapid rate for several decades and further local extirpations are being prevented through intensive conservation action.
documentation.population: An estimate of the total minimum population size was derived from male lek counts in 2015, when 85,674 males were counted on 3,559 known leks (WAFWA 2015). Mark-resight approaches suggest lek count maxima represent c. 58% of males attending a lek (including yearling males: 68% were adults), implying 148,998 males were associated with known leks across the whole range in 2015 (WAFWA 2015). The study then used a weighted average of 1.85 females to males to extrapolate a total of 424,645 individuals (WAFWA 2015). Using 0.68 for the proportion of adult birds, a minimum population size in 2015 was 288,759, rounded here to 289,000 mature individuals. This value doesn’t account for unknown leks: in Colorado it was thought 80% of males were known. While the proportion of unknown leks varies with the population size in each state, if we assume that this value applies across the range then a precautionary population size would be around 350,000. An upper bound is highly uncertain, but it seems unlikely that known males are less than half the population size, and a tentative upper value of 550,000 mature individuals is inferred here.
documentation.habitats:
It is closely associated with sagebrush Artemesia habitats during the breeding and non-breeding seasons, although some populations do undergo seasonal movements (del Hoyo et al. 1994, Schroeder et al. 1999). It is a lekking species. It may act as an umbrella to other sage-brush specialists when conserved.
The interaction between the spread of invasive grasses and increased fire frequency causes ongoing loss and degradation of the sagebrush habitat on which the species depends. There are further impacts recorded from the expansion of conifer forest, human development and over-abundant grazers (Remington et al. 2021). Despite a concerted and large-scale multi-stakeholder response to address sagebrush loss, these threats continue to affect the range. An ongoing decline in the area, extent and in the quality of the species’ habitat is inferred.
documentation.threats:
The long-standing population declines are due in general to the loss and degradation of sagebrush habitat, which has been driven by conversion for agriculture, energy infrastructure development, road building and other residential and industrial development (Walker et al. 2007, USFWS-DOI 2010, USFWS 2013, Remington et al. 2021). Immense areas of its habitat have been cleared or degraded due to cultivation (for wheat, potatoes and other crops), burning and overgrazing, and the species has been extirpated from various parts of its former range (British Columbia, Nebraska, Kansas, Oklahoma, New Mexico and Arizona) (Schroeder et al. 1999). Continuing development of natural gas resources is causing reduced lek attendance and overall population (Holloran and Anderson 2005). 
Separate broad-scale factors driving loss of habitat are those that encourage the expansion of conifers and invasive grasses (e.g. cheatgrass), notably increased fire frequency and intensity (Davies et al. 2011, USFWS 2013, Doherty et al. 2021, Remington et al. 2021, Coates et al. 2024), but also improper grazing regimes (USFWS 2013).
Levels of hunting of the species are tightly regulated, but may still limit potential population growth with larger populations found to respond positively to hunting closures (Dinkins et al. 2021). Detecting the impacts of even low levels of hunting is challenging, and they may not be clear from current monitoring focused on lek attendance (Dinkins et al. 2021).
Coyote Canis latrans control is likely to have a detrimental impact on sage grouse owing to the loss of beneficial indirect interactions (Mezquida et al. 2006).
In 2003, about 25% of the radio-marked sage-grouse in the Powder River Basin died from West Nile virus. That number dropped to 10% in 2004 and 2% in 2005 in response to cool summer temperatures, but the long-term impacts require further study (Walker et al. 2007b).
documentation.measures:
Conservation Actions Underway
The species occurs within a number of protected areas and has been the focus of extensive ecological study. Management recommendations have been made to minimise the impacts of natural gas exploitation in sagebrush habitat (Holloran and Anderson 2005) and the Western Governor's Association are developing a strategy to minimise the impacts of development on sage grouse populations. A total of 63 Sage Grouse Local Working Groups have been established within its range, bringing stakeholders together to plan and implement local level conservation actions.

Conservation Actions Proposed
Adopt best practice methods when developing gas fields. Continue to monitor population trends. Manage the sage-brush ecosystem in a way that is beneficial to other habitat specialists and restores natural food-webs.
documentation.use_trade: High levels of market hunting in the early 20th Century are thought to have limited and reduced populations (Schroeder et al. 1999). Hunting is still permitted in Montana, Wyoming, Colorado, Utah, Idaho, Nevada, and Oregon, but is restricted to 5-10% of recorded population size and supplies funding for conservation efforts through hunting permit charges (Dinkins et al. 2021). Very low levels of hunting appear to be compatible with the persistence of populations where carefully monitored, however impacts may not be readily detectable and could still represent a contributing factor in declines: larger populations appear to respond positively to hunting closures, suggesting there is a role of hunting in limiting population growth but this was not consistently true for small populations (Dinkins et al. 2021).
documentation.rationale: This species is listed as Vulnerable owing to a long-standing, continuing rapid decline in its population that has seen the range contract and the species approach extirpation in Canada. It is intrinsically connected to sagebrush habitat, and declines are primarily due to sagebrush loss and degradation for agriculture and development, but encroaching conifers and fire-adapted invasive grasses have accelerated sagebrush degradation through increasing fire frequency and intensity. Ongoing conservation efforts are crucial to prevent the further acceleration of decline rates.
documentation.trend_justification:
Range-wide monitoring data collected at leks since 1960 have been consolidated into a single dataset (O’Donnell et al. 2021) and analysed using a state-space model to derive the most likely rates of population change subsequently updated with new data (Coates et al. 2023, Prochazka et al. 2024). This trend analysis, using data from across the whole extent of the species’ distribution, modelled that the population has declined by a consistent rate of 2.9-3.0 % per year for three different timeframes based on population nadirs, implying declines of 41.1, 64.5 and 78.4 % relative to population sizes 19, 35 and 55 years earlier respectively (Prochazka et al. 2024). A consistent and rapid rate of population reduction is evident, at a rate equivalent to 37.9-42.4 % over three generations. While this is the best available index for tracking population change, lek count data cannot provide an estimated rate of continuing decline as the degree to which the data match true population size and trend is uncertain (Walsh et al. 2004, 2010, Shyvers et al. 2020), despite refinements of the analysis (Coates et al. 2023, Prochazka et al. 2024).
Separately, Audubon Christmas Bird Count (CBC) data covering about a quarter of the wintering range shows an annual rate of decline between 8.4% (0.9-15.9 %) over the past 19 years, with the probability of decline greater than 30 % over this time of 0.96 (T. Meehan in litt. 2025).
Notwithstanding localised success in preventing extirpation through direct conservation action, there seems little evidence that this long-term trend is about to be reversed given the high probabilities of extinction assigned to leks across the range (Prochazka et al. 2024), and accordingly this rapid reduction is projected to continue. These long-standing declines are due in general to the loss and degradation of sagebrush habitat, which have been driven by conversion for agriculture, energy infrastructure development, road building and other residential and industrial development (Walker et al. 2007a, USFWS-DOI 2010, USFWS 2013, Remington et al. 2021). Separately broader scale factors driving loss of habitat are those that encourage the expansion of conifers and invasive grasses, notably increased fire frequency and intensity (Davies et al. 2011, USFWS 2013, Doherty et al. 2021, Remington et al. 2021, Coates et al. 2024), but also improper grazing regimes (USFWS 2013).
